title: Finn's Wobbly Plan
markdown:
Atherton College’s common room smelled of polished oak and lamp oil. It was the night of the Annual Curators’ Society vote, a solemn affair that Elara the hedgehog, ceramics assistant and creature of exquisite precision, had planned down to the last ballot and the last chair. Her quills vibrated. Lamplight spilled like warm honey.

“Now, Finn,” she murmured to her stoat friend, who was, for the third time, rearranging the name cards. “The seating chart is final. Utterly. Irrevocably.”

Finn paused mid-twitch. “But this one’s a tad wobbly. A loose thread can unravel the whole tapestry of civility.”

“It is a name card. The vote concerns the Luminous Amethyst vase, not the structural integrity of cardstock.”

Therefore the cards stayed, slightly crooked, and the distinguished cavalcade arrived: Professor Sterling the ornithologist, scarf already migrating; Professor Albright the botanist, stern as a labelled fern. Elara nodded. Stage Two: discreet distribution of voting slips.

But a rogue gust, entirely unpredicted, found a window that had no business being open. It danced through the stacked slips with impish glee. Chaos threatened.

Therefore Finn leapt. “A rogue draft. Fear not. I shall corral these wayward documents.” He scrambled onto a table and batted at fluttering papers, which spun further. Elara’s compass spun with them. Finn cornered a ballot by the grand fireplace, scooped it, and nudged an exquisitely carved urn. It tumbled with a soft clatter into crumpled manifestos.

“Finn,” Elara hissed, a sound that could curdle milk.

Murmurs grew. Albright raised a skeptical eyebrow. The plan was unravelling through well-intentioned blunders, not malice. Finn then “secured” the remaining slips beneath a bust of the college founder. The bust began to tilt.

But they still had to present the vase. It came forward shimmering, otherworldly. The room’s exasperation told another story. Finn, in a desperate bid to impress, tried to balance the amethyst on an overturned waste bin.

Therefore, in that teetering moment, Elara did something uncharacteristic. She let go. The perfect plan was collapsing with theatrical flourish, and she chose not to chase the last card.

“Finn. Stop. Everyone. Please. Just stop.”

A collective pause. Eyes found her. Spines softened.

“My plan was too rigid. Too intent on perfection. Finn, your heart is in the right place. In the frantic effort to fix every tiny detail we miss the grander picture.” She looked at the faces, the tilted bust, the urn in the paper nest. “Instead of performing certainty, we could simply ask for help. Truly ask. Then listen. Together.”

Sterling blinked and adjusted his scarf. “I happen to know a method for securing delicate objects: reinforced twine and a cleverly positioned counterweight.”

Albright piped up. “I have vine cuttings, strong and flexible. An exceptionally stable base.”

Finn, sheepish, nodded hard. “I can fetch anything. Tell me what you actually need.”

Therefore ideas flowed—not chaos, a stream. Finn, under Elara’s direction, brought twine. Elara, freed from the first plan, helped devise the counterweight. The Luminous Amethyst sat safe at last, not by flawless choreography but by shared work. The vote, when it came, was smooth. Finn beamed. Elara’s quills were still. The common room, which had been all honey-light and wobble, kept a vase that no longer required a waste bin, and a pair of friends who had learned to ask before they piled paper under statues.
